items.title: Southern California port employers, watchmen union reach tentative deal
items.content_html:
Nov 21 (Reuters) - The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) employers group at the Los Angeles and Long Beach ports said on Saturday it had reached a tentative agreement with the union for security guards, averting a strike that could have disrupted operations at the two busiest cargo shipping hubs in the US.

The International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 represents 250 security officers, or watchmen, who account for a small fraction of the ports' workforce, but their work is critical because they control access at terminal gates, conduct security patrols and report safety issues.

PMA, which represents terminal owners, said the agreement reached on Saturday was subject to ratification by Local 26 members, and the current contract will be extended pending ratification.

The union did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside regular business hours.

The two sides resumed federally mediated negotiations on Friday, two days after the parties broke off talks, with the employers group reporting "little-to-no movement from the union on PMA's proposals."

The PMA said at the time that its offer included a one-time bonus of $3,200 for each union member and a wage proposal that would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000.

The offer also called for maintaining fully employer-paid healthcare for active workers and retirees, valued at more than $62,000 each year, and increased pension benefits up to $93,200 a year for workers with the longest tenure.

Talks between the terminal owners and the union have stretched on for more than a year.

Reporting by Akanksha Khushi in Bengaluru, Steve Gorman and Lisa Baertlein in Los Angeles. Editing by Toby Chopra and Mark Potter

items.title: As e-bike battery fires mount, New York weighs tougher restrictions
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 21 (Reuters) - They lean in apartment hallways, charge overnight in bedrooms and carry many of New York City's delivered meals. Increasingly, they are also a source of fires, linked to aging or inferior batteries.

The deaths of 10 people in two recent New York fires — at least one of them determined to be caused by e-bike batteries — prompted the New York City Council to hold an emergency hearing on Friday on a raft of stricter rules for e-bike storage and battery safety.

The three-hour meeting highlighted growing concerns among city residents about the surge in lithium-ion battery fires, which are up about 70% from a year ago. Among other measures, the proposed legislation would make it a crime to possess or use batteries that do not meet safety standards and would ban storing batteries inside apartments.

It is unclear whether the measures will advance. Officials in Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration, including from the New York City Fire Department, criticized the proposals, saying they would penalize everyday riders and low-income delivery workers.

Fire Department Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the administration had "significant concerns of unintended consequences that would most heavily impact delivery workers, many of whom are immigrants, with limited English proficiency."

Delivery workers "could face losing their livelihoods and having their lives upended through the confiscation of the device they use every day to make a living," she said.

Lithium-ion battery fires have become an international concern since e-bikes and e-scooters soared in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic. Many of those batteries are now aging, which fire officials say is likely adding to the number of fires.

Governments have taken different approaches. Britain, for instance, has focused on sellers of batteries and devices that use them.

"Unsafe e-bike and e-scooter batteries pose a serious fire risk, which is why we're strengthening the responsibility of online marketplaces and working with local authorities to remove unsafe products from sale," a British government spokesperson said in response to Reuters questions.

In the United States, the Senate unanimously passed legislation on Thursday sponsored by New York's senators, Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand, that would direct the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set mandatory safety standards for lithium-ion batteries used in e-bikes and other micromobility devices. The commission proposed mandatory safety standards for the batteries in June, after a public meeting in 2023. The House of Representatives has already passed the bill.

A commission staff report published in April found 45 deaths from 2017 to 2024 linked to lithium-ion battery fires involving micromobility devices: 19 tied to e-bikes, 15 to e-scooters and 11 to self-balancing scooters or hoverboards.

The issue is particularly acute in New York, where lithium-ion battery fires have reached a record this year. There were 406 such fires through early November, up from 241 in the same period last year, according to Fire Department figures cited by the City Council.

On October 28, an e-bike battery ignited in an apartment in a public housing project in the Bronx, killing four people including an 11-year-old boy. The e-bike was near the doorway, blocking the family's escape, Bonsignore said at the time.

About a week later, a fire in Sunset Park, a working-class Brooklyn neighborhood, killed six people and injured at least seven. Investigators have not determined the cause, but fire officials said two charred e-bikes were removed from the building and batteries were found in debris.

"The recent building fires in Sunset Park and in the South Bronx, which collectively claimed the lives of 10 New Yorkers, are heartbreaking tragedies that underscore the urgent need for action to prevent further loss of life," City Council Speaker Julie Menin said at the time.

Reporting by Maria Tsvetkova and Nichola Groom; Additional reporting by Barbara Lewis; Editing by William Mallard

items.title: Most new Black Democrats in decades to join US Congress, set to sway policy, party
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 21 (Reuters) - The largest class of new Black Democratic lawmakers in more than 30 years will join the US Congress in January after November's midterm elections despite Republican-led redistricting efforts, according to a Reuters analysis.

The electoral outcome sets up a test of whether increased Black representation can translate into legislative power.

Congress will include 13 new Black Democratic members, the largest cohort since 1993, House historian data showed. Four are 34 years old or younger, and more than half of Black House members were first seated in 2021 or later.

The influx of Black lawmakers could reshape Congress' legislative priorities on voting rights, healthcare affordability and economic inequality, while giving a new generation of leaders a greater voice in shaping Democratic policy, political observers say. But the lawmakers' influence will depend on whether they can translate their growing numbers into powerful committee assignments and legislative victories at a time when longstanding civil rights protections face mounting challenges.

Black candidates won 58 seats in the 435-member House for the 120th Congress, down from 61 in the current Congress, with two additional Black candidates in Louisiana headed to December 12 runoffs. Four Black Republicans will depart Congress, leaving US Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina as the only Black Republican in either chamber. Black representation in the Senate reached a record seven members following the election of Democrat Juliana Stratton in Illinois and the upset victory by Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom.

The shift in representation echoes the 1990s, when efforts to expand Black political representation helped usher in a new generation of lawmakers — many of whom have since gained seniority and influence, said Dedrick Asante-Muhammad, president of the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies.

"This points to how important it was for a significant increase in Black representatives and how it pays off 20 to 30 years later," Asante-Muhammad said.

DIVERSE REPRESENTATION

In 1993, 16 first-time Black members joined when Congress convened, and 17 had joined by the end, the most of any Congress. Five of the current six longest-serving Black House members were first seated in 1991 or 1993.

"When you have proportional representation in Congress, it does allow for diverse representation across committees. Part of the reason why the Congressional Black Caucus formed is so that they could convince leadership to put Blacks on key committees," said Andra Gillespie, a professor at Emory University who studies African American leadership in politics.

All current members of the caucus are Democrats.

"We're all being contacted by our constituents who are impressing upon us the need to be very bold in our approach ... to address what are crises in communities across the country," said caucus chair, US Representative Yvette Clarke, a New York Democrat, citing the affordability crisis as its members' main concern.

REDRAWN MAPS

Four districts held by Black Democrats were among those that Republican-led legislatures redrew to try to gain seats, in a push that intensified after the Supreme Court's April ruling that weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Republicans have flipped none of the three decided so far.

Democrats Shomari Figures and Don Davis won reelection to the House in Alabama and North Carolina, respectively, while Democrat Leticia Gutierrez, who does not identify as Black, won a redrawn district in Texas previously held by Democrat Al Green.

Two Black women have a chance to secure Louisiana's remaining two congressional seats. In a majority-Black Louisiana district redrawn in May, Democrat Chauna Banks will face Republican Blake Miguez in a December 12 runoff. In a neighboring district, Democrat Patricia Moore, who led a nine-candidate field with nearly 18% of the vote, will take on Republican Gabe Firment, who received 17.2%.

US Senator Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democrat and the 11th Black senator in US history, told Reuters lawmakers must begin shaping their policy agenda before Congress convenes in January. Warnock donated to and campaigned for Colom, who will be Mississippi's first Black senator in more than 140 years.

"I'm focused on ending this war, ending these tariffs, and restoring tax credits that will bring people's healthcare costs down," Warnock said.

Most major legislation will still require bipartisan support in the Senate, and Republican President Donald Trump can veto bills passed by Congress.

NEW FACES, SENIOR LEADERS AND A TEST FOR DEMOCRATS

Black Democrats' leverage will depend on a delegation that is newer, and in some cases much younger, than in the last Congress. Melat Kiros, 29, is the first woman from Gen Z — the generation born between the late 1990s and the early 2010s — elected to Congress and the first Black woman to represent Colorado. She is one of four first-time Black House members who are 34 or younger, alongside Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Adrian Boafo of Maryland, both 32, and Donavan McKinney of Michigan, 34. In contrast, the Democratic caucus' senior Black leaders include US Representatives Maxine Waters of California, 88, and Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, 78.

"I'm unapologetically progressive. So many people are looking for bold leadership and I think that too often the messages that come out are that boldness is risky," said reelected US Representative Summer Lee, a Black Pennsylvania Democrat.

The generational mix will be tested at the top, where US Representative Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat and the favorite to become House speaker, would manage a caucus that includes moderates and progressives seeking to move the party beyond its established leadership.

"Democratic leadership is in for some trouble. (Senate Democratic leader Chuck) Schumer and Jeffries are really going to have to push back against what is going to be and has already proven to be a groundswell against their leadership," said Periloux Peay, a political science professor at the University of Maryland.

The Congressional Black Caucus will enter the new session with a record 64 members, up from 62. Chair Clarke said she is focused on aligning progressives and moderates and expressed confidence in Jeffries.

"I'm under the impression that he's not tone deaf and that he will lead as the body requires," Clarke said.

items.title: FBI's criminal information database hacked, CNN reports
items.content_html:
Nov 20 (Reuters) - The FBI is investigating a suspected breach of a nationwide database used by federal, state and local law enforcement agencies to share criminal justice information, CNN reported on Friday, citing two people briefed on the investigation.

The apparent compromise of the National Crime Information Center database would mark the second intrusion involving an FBI system in recent months and the latest in a string of cyber incidents that have alarmed US officials over the past week.

The agency did not respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

The FBI database is used by law enforcement agencies nationwide to store and share information on warrants, criminal histories and background checks.

Previous high-profile cyber disruptions over the past week have included a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.

A September breach by a digital extortion group known as "ShinyHunters" accessed an FBI jobs website, compromising data on current and former FBI employees.

Reporting by Nathan Layne, Costas Pitas and Jasper Ward; Editing by William Mallard and Sergio Non

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Nvidia's accounting is a focus of US SEC investigation, sources say
items.content_html:
NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia's accounting practices, said two people briefed on the matter, adding to the legal woes facing the scandal-hit chip giant.

The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday reported that the SEC was probing Nvidia but said it could not ascertain the focus of the investigation. The people, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential issues, said SEC enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues at the company.

A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Prices of Nvidia shares extended losses and were down about 13% on Friday, according to LSEG data, after Reuters reported details of the SEC probe. They had been down more than 6% before Reuters published its report.

Reuters could not immediately determine when the SEC opened its inquiry or exactly what potential accounting issues the watchdog is examining. Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action.

Still, the accounting focus of the probe, which Reuters is reporting for the first time, increases pressure on Nvidia, whose investors are still reeling from revelations about ousted CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital relationships, including with Alice Huang, who US authorities suspect is a Chinese spy. China has denied she is a spy.

Alice Huang led Singapore-based Megaspeed, historically a large Nvidia chip customer, people familiar with the matter have said. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week.

The crisis has sent shares in Nvidia, a linchpin of the AI boom, tumbling more than a third and stoked calls in Washington for tougher action on tech threats posed by Beijing.

Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it conducted "lawful business." Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a November 8 statement following the reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, without referring to her by name.

The SEC probe is the latest of Nvidia's legal woes. The Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia's $12.9-billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company's acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported last month.

SINGAPORE ACCOUNTING CHANGE BACK IN FOCUS

Last year, Nvidia changed how it reports geographic revenue, using customer headquarters rather than billing addresses, which it said would better reflect the geographic profile of its revenue. The change resulted in Singapore being removed from its geographical breakdown.

The Financial Times, citing company accounts, reported on Tuesday that Nvidia had made the change even as Singapore sales soared to almost half its global revenue.

That accounting shift has drawn renewed press scrutiny in the wake of the Alice Huang scandal.

Southeast Asia has become a hub for chip smuggling to China since the Biden administration barred advanced AI chip exports to that country over concerns they could boost Beijing's military.

Analysts and investors have also grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centers. Nvidia has backed AI companies and cloud providers and provided guarantees connected to data-center projects that use its equipment.

Critics say such arrangements can make it harder for investors to assess the quality of chipmakers' revenue and their true financial exposure. Speaking to Reuters last month, SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks.

On its Tuesday earnings call, Nvidia's interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more selective moving forward about AI industry financing deals.

The SEC under President Donald Trump has pulled back on enforcement, saying it will focus on bread-and-butter securities fraud, including accounting violations that have long been a mainstay of its enforcement work. It recently launched a new financial reporting and accounting unit within its enforcement division, aimed at developing cases in accounting and auditing areas.

(This story has been refiled to correct Nvidia's RIC in paragraph 1.)

Reporting by Chris Prentice in New York and Alexandra Alper in Washington; Additional reporting by Karen Freifeld and Jody Godoy in New York; Editing by Michelle Price and Daniel Wallis

items.title: Texas prisoner moans in pain for minutes during unusual lethal injection, witnesses say
items.content_html:
Nov 20 (Reuters) - A condemned Texas prisoner moaned and yelled out in pain and remained conscious for several minutes after prison officials began administering lethal injections in what witnesses described on Friday as an unusually protracted execution.

Prison officials took about 34 minutes to successfully insert two intravenous lines in convicted murderer Reinaldo Dennes: one in his neck and the other in his left foot after the veins in his arms were found unviable, according to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice.

They began injecting pentobarbital, a caustic barbiturate, at 6:52 p.m. on Thursday, and he was declared dead 15 minutes later, according to the department's records, during which a media witness and a spiritual adviser said Dennes repeatedly moaned in pain.

The spiritual adviser, the Rev. Jeff Hood, recalled Dennes using repeated expletives and saying: "My leg is killing me," and, "My leg it's on fire, it's on fire."

"He was clearly in tremendous distress," Hood, who was inside the execution chamber with his hand on Dennes' shoulder, told reporters. "Twice he said 'it's not working, it's not working, it's not going how it's supposed to go.'"

Hood, who has witnessed 13 executions by lethal injection, told reporters he had not previously seen "anyone able to make complete sentences past 30 seconds."

Public scrutiny of the decades-old execution method has been renewed after Christa Pike, convicted of murder, survived Tennessee's attempt to execute her using pentobarbital in September, leaving her badly injured and unconscious for several days.

And it comes as newly elected Democratic politicians take over some Texas offices in January in what had long been a Republican stronghold, including Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect, who says she opposes capital punishment.

Hood said four or five minutes passed before Dennes' breathing began to slow to heavy gurgling and snoring sounds and he appeared to lose consciousness.

Amanda Hernandez, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, said the execution followed Texas protocol, from his being strapped to the gurney at 6:04 p.m. to the declaration of death at 7:07 p.m., just over an hour later.

"It was not a botched execution, it proceeded as planned and it was successful," she said in an interview.

Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press journalist who has been a media witness at nearly 500 executions since the 1980s, said the execution of Dennes was "dramatically different."

He said that Dennes, convicted of murdering diamond wholesaler Janos Szucs during a robbery in 1996, moaned of "excruciating pain." He said that over about three minutes, Dennes, a Christian, repeatedly called out: "Take me, Father! Take me into your arms."

Reporting by Jonathan Allen in New York; editing by Paul Thomasch and Rosalba O'Brien

items.title: Backing Trump, US Senate Republicans block Iran war resolution
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - US Senate Republicans on Thursday rejected legislation directing President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran or obtain Congress' approval to continue, backing the president weeks after sweeping defeats in midterm elections largely tied to Americans' frustration with the conflict.

The Senate voted 51 to 48, largely along party lines, to defeat a war powers resolution that had previously passed the House of Representatives.

The US Constitution says that only Congress, not the president, can declare war, and Democrats have argued that Trump may have pulled the country into a long conflict by failing to spell out a clear strategy.

Only three Republicans - Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky - voted with Democrats in favor of the resolution. One Democrat, John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, voted with Republicans against it.

The vote was the first on the conflict since Democratic victories in the midterm elections on November 3. Trump's fellow Republicans, who rarely break with the president, stood behind him in support of the US-Israeli war on Iran that started on February 28.

Just 31% of Americans approve of the US war on Iran, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted November 13-16.

It was the 21st vote in Congress on a war powers resolution since the war began. Democrats said they filed the measure to put Republicans on the record as supporting the war.

SHOWDOWN LOOMS IN 2027

Democrats will control large majorities in the House and Senate next year, and party leaders have pledged to make ending the war a top priority once they take over on January 3, setting the stage for a potential showdown with Trump.

Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia, who has called repeatedly for Congress to take back its control over declarations of war, said the midterm election result reflected Americans' unhappiness about the war, and higher prices for food, fuel and other goods linked to the conflict.

"Its unpopularity was made absolutely, manifestly clear in the election results of November 3," Kaine said in a speech before the vote appealing for yes votes.

Democrats made affordability a theme of the election campaign.

Democrats have also balked at the cost of the foreign conflict, at a time when Republicans have been cutting domestic programs like health insurance subsidies and free school lunches.

Pentagon data in late October showed that the US military had spent over $47 billion to prosecute the war, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department's estimate in July.

The latest resolution had passed the House in mid-September by 220-204, reflecting lawmakers' growing unhappiness with the months-long conflict weeks before the midterms.

A similar measure passed both the Senate and House earlier this year, but the Trump administration ignored it, saying it was not legally binding.

Reporting by Patricia Zengerle; Editing by Don Durfee and Alistair Bell

items.title: Anthropic's Tom Brown plans to donate to Trump's investment accounts for kids, source says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Anthropic (ANT.O) co-founder Tom Brown will donate to US President Donald Trump's cradle-to-adulthood investment program known as Trump Accounts, according to a source familiar with the donation, joining a slew of wealthy individuals supporting the initiative.

Anthropic raised $93.5 billion in its blockbuster IPO on Thursday after underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares.

Brown's donation is the latest sign of Anthropic's effort to improve relations with the Trump administration. The AI developer and its CEO, Dario Amodei, have at times clashed with Trump and senior administration officials over AI policy. In recent months, Brown, Anthropic's chief compute officer, has emerged as a key liaison to the administration, appearing at a technology-focused G20 event hosted by the US in August and at the September launch of a government AI tool.

Trump at a press conference on Friday said he has "a lot of respect" for Amodei, a signal that the president's relationship with the company is improving.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent separately said in an interview with CNBC on Friday that an Anthropic founder would donate to the program "over the next few weeks," without naming Brown.

Trump Accounts provide government-funded investment accounts of $1,000 to US citizens born between 2025 and 2028. The program aims to promote investing and financial literacy from an early age.

attachments.title: Anthropic holds IPO at the NASDAQ MarketSite in Times Square

items.title: Former Nvidia CEO Huang agreed to testify at public US Senate hearing, senator's aide says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Former Nvidia (NVDA.O) CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the US Senate in a public hearing, an aide to Republican US Senator Tim Scott said in a statement on Friday, as lawmakers probe allegations about Huang's ties to a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

Huang has drawn increased attention from US lawmakers since the New York Times reported he had a romantic relationship with the woman, raising questions on exports of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China.

If the hearing proceeds as planned, it would mark Huang's first public testimony since stepping down as Nvidia's chief executive on November 12.

A spokesperson for Huang declined to comment on the hearing. Scott's office did not provide a date, though the senator's original request asked Huang to appear on December 3.

Huang separately agreed to a closed-door interview with three House committees, slated for December 1.

Reporting by Courtney Rozen; editing by Deepa Babington

items.title: US Vice President Vance declines to say he would have ordered Iran strikes
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - US Vice President JD Vance on Friday declined to say whether he would have authorized strikes on Iran to prevent the country from developing a nuclear weapon, sidestepping President Donald Trump's calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again.

Speaking at a White House press conference alongside Trump, Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February was Trump's call, "and my job is to support the president of the United States."

The answer underscored the delicate balancing act the vice president and his party face as the Iran conflict creates domestic political challenges.

In a blunt midterm election postmortem, Vance blamed the war for Republicans' historic losses and called for the US to exit the conflict. Many viewed his statement, posted on social media, as a break with Trump as the vice president considers a 2028 White House bid.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote. "The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay."

Trump on Friday said he was not unhappy with Vance's conclusion, but said it lacked a crucial element: an acknowledgment that the strikes were necessary and that Vance would make the same decision.

"People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion," Trump said. "But I say, I know the Iranians, and, frankly, they're crazy."

When asked later in the press conference if the war was worth Republicans' steep congressional losses, Vance did not explicitly endorse the operation.

"What I've said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing," Vance said. "It's the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage, or, God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, potentially of innocent people.

"And I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States."

Vance has long opposed the war and acted as Washington's main emissary for peace talks, brokering a short-lived provisional truce over the summer that quickly fell apart.

In recent weeks, he sent personal correspondence to hardliners in Tehran to restart negotiations. But Trump called off the engagements shortly after Vance published his post-campaign assessment, telling the vice president to focus on domestic policy.

"We don't need a deal with Iran," Trump wrote on social media, announcing his direction to Vance. "Those days have long since passed."

Trump returned on Thursday from a four-day diplomatic trip through Asia, which culminated in an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump faced criticism for meeting — and exchanging warm greetings — with both leaders. He hugged Xi after landing in China and called Putin "my friend."

White House officials cast the meeting as a show of mature statesmanship, arguing that Trump's relationships, even with US adversaries, displayed Washington's global strength.

Vance, who remained in Washington, was the trip's chief cheerleader. He quipped during the press conference that remaining stateside during Trump's mission was like the 1990 family comedy film "Home Alone."

"It's amazing what's possible when you give diplomacy a real chance," he wrote Thursday on social media.

items.title: Trump says Democrats facing veto power should work with him
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump pledged on Friday to veto legislation passed by Democrats when they take control of Congress in 2027, but said his veto power should be seen as a starting point for lawmakers who want to achieve change.

Speaking at a White House news conference, Trump called the presidential veto "extreme powers," and said his threat to block legislation would cause Democrats to moderate their policies.

"They're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them. And then they're going to send more things, and I'm going to veto them," Trump said. "And they could go two years and one month, because that's what we have, and I'm going to veto them."

Trump said Democrats may realize that to avoid his veto, they could work with him to accomplish legislative goals.

"Because of the power of the veto, there's a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done," he said.

Trump said many Democrats had called him to discuss healthcare and immigration reform and pointed to healthcare as an area where lawmakers from different perspectives might meet somewhere in the middle.

"I'm open to great healthcare now, especially on healthcare. I'm open to great healthcare now," he said.

"Can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country."

With the new Congress set to choose its leadership soon, Trump described Senator Chuck Schumer, who is vying to become senate majority leader, and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who is on the path to becoming the next house speaker, both from New York, as "smart" and expressed willingness to work together.

"If they want to get things done, I want to get things done too," Trump said.

Trump also said Democratic Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa had called him two days ago about the border and he thought they could find a solution.

"She was really nice. It was a very productive call, and she wants to have a strong border. And we'll be able. I think we'll be able to work something out," he said.

items.title: Trump says he still backs Lutnick, urges Nvidia's Huang to apologize
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Friday he still supported Howard Lutnick, calling him "a very good businessman" as a scandal at AI chipmaker Nvidia (NVDA.O) raises questions about Lutnick's handling of Chinese chip sales.

Trump, speaking to reporters at a press conference following his trip to Asia this week, also said he discussed Nvidia's co-founder and now-former CEO Jensen Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping but gave no other details about their conversation.

Reports that Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a company executive and ties to a suspected Chinese spy triggered his resignation and sparked investigations by US regulators and the FBI, congressional action, an internal review and a proposed investor class-action lawsuit.

US Senator Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican, told the Wall Street Journal earlier on Friday that Lutnick repeatedly ignored warnings that US artificial-intelligence chips were being smuggled to China before the Nvidia scandal became public but stopped short of saying he should resign.

Democrats, who take over Congress in January, meanwhile are probing whether Lutnick used his office to help investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald, which is controlled by his sons, avoid losses stemming from scrutiny of Nvidia's ties to a Chinese firm.

"I have not lost confidence. He's a different kind of a guy, very good businessman," Trump told reporters. "I think he's doing a very good job."

Trump also said he'd like to see the former Nvidia chief "make a big apology and go back," adding: "I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant — he's a brilliant man.' He is."

His comments contradict those by his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC in an interview earlier on Friday that the former Nvidia CEO did not come up in talks.

The New York Times reported on Friday that the suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, has extensive ties to China's defense industry.

Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the US Senate in a public hearing, an aide to the Senate Banking chairman said on Friday, though a representative for Huang declined to comment. Huang is also scheduled to speak to US House lawmakers behind closed doors in early December.

items.title: Indian man sentenced to more than 19 years in US for plotting to kill Sikh separatist
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 20 (Reuters) - An Indian man was sentenced to more than 19 years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York City, in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents.

Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

US District Judge Victor Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence at a hearing in Manhattan federal court.

The discovery of alleged assassination plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India, which has denied involvement in such plots.

Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice in New York, who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.

Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who was actually an undercover US law enforcement officer, court papers show.

Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear whether he has hired a defense lawyer.

India's government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.

Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney's office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.

"This case cuts to the very core of American values," prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court. "We don't condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever."

Addressing the court on Friday, Gupta said he regretted straying from the nonviolent example set by Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.

"I'm sorry to Mr. Pannun, I'm sorry to the communities I hurt, I'm sorry to my own family," Gupta said.

Pannun told the court that he was grateful to the US for prosecuting Gupta and said he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.

"Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal," he said.

Reporting by Luc Cohen in New York; Editing by Alistair Bell

attachments.title: Nikhil Gupta, accused by US federal prosecutors of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a US resident who advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India, stands as he is sentenced by US District Judge Victor Marrero in federal court in New York City, US, November 20, 2026 in this courtroom sketch. REUTERS/Jane Rosenberg

items.title: Trump touts Asia trade deal wins, but US agricultural exports disappoint
items.content_html:
Summary:

  • Reuters analysis of 10 deals finds promised farm export gains often fail to materialize
  • China's non-soy farm purchases remain far below Beijing's post-May summit pledge
  • Export bumps after deal announcements often faded, weakening claims of lasting farmer benefits

CHICAGO, Nov 20 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump visited Asia this week, boasting of a string of agricultural trade victories since threatening to impose tariffs that would decimate other countries' trade.

US trade agreements have at times buoyed prices of crops and livestock, but a Reuters analysis of 10 deals showed few have generated a promised windfall of US farm product sales.

China, the largest US trading partner in Asia, appears on track to meet its commitment to buy 25 million metric tons of US soybeans in 2026, but purchases remain below levels seen before Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs in April 2025. Beijing's agreement to buy $17 billion worth of other US farm products this year is largely unfulfilled.

The data undercuts White House messaging that Trump's trade tactics are benefiting US farmers and ushering in what the president has called a "golden age" of agriculture. Dissatisfaction over the president's tariff strategy contributed to losses for Trump's Republican Party in this month's midterm elections, including among farmers who voted for Trump, analysts say.

The Trump administration says it has secured around a dozen trade deals with Asian countries since imposing tariffs, easing plant and livestock health requirements for incoming US products and expanding low-tariff import quotas. Some included minimum annual purchase commitments for US crops and meat.

But agricultural exports to partner nations often increased immediately following White House announcements before tapering off, the Reuters analysis found.

"The reality is that this has been a lot of talk and not much action," said Scott Lincicome, vice president of economics and trade at the Cato Institute think tank.

During Trump's Asia trip this week, he said the US reached a "very big trade deal" with the Philippines. Manila said, however, the two countries had reached an understanding on economic cooperation.

MISSED TARGETS

Some deals have been finalized, but have not met their targets.

Indonesia, the 12th-largest US agricultural products importer by value, agreed in February to import $4.5 billion of farm goods. But in the first nine months of 2026, US exports totaled less than $2.4 billion, roughly in line with the same period over the last decade, according to US Census Bureau trade data.

Indonesia agreed to import 3.5 million tons of US soybeans annually, but just 54% of that goal had shipped as of September, the trade data showed. Wheat exports of less than 450,000 tons represented less than a quarter of Indonesia's annual commitment, while soymeal exports of just 150,000 tons made up 4% of a 3.8-million-ton target.

The White House said a trade agreement with Malaysia, signed in October 2025, would provide US exporters "unprecedented access" to its market. The deal promised to open market access for US sorghum and facilitate pork and poultry exports. However, 2026 US pork exports through September were down 52% from the same period a year earlier, while there were zero poultry and sorghum shipments, US government data showed.

The text of a February trade deal with Bangladesh, following Trump's threat of tariffs that could devastate the South Asian nation's textiles industry, stated that the country or companies there would buy at least 700,000 tons of US wheat annually for five years and $1.25 billion worth or 2.6 million tons of soy and soy products over one year. Since then, US wheat exports totaled 473,000 tons while combined soybean and soymeal shipments reached just 162,000 tons, US government data showed.

Trade talks with China have shown mixed results. Trump met on Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen after a brief stop in the Philippines for a Southeast Asian summit.

The world's top soybean importer halted purchases from the US last year as the trade war heated up, but resumed modest purchases after talks in Busan, South Korea, last October and in Beijing in May. But China has not lifted its 10% tariff on US soybeans, so government buyers booked the nearly 20 million tons from the current US harvest. Private Chinese importers continued to buy from rival supplier Brazil.

The White House said it secured a deal for Beijing to buy $17 billion of other US agricultural goods annually, with this year's target prorated. But the US has exported less than $2.5 billion of US farm goods, excluding soybeans, to China since the May summit through September, US government data showed.

In a statement, the White House said China has achieved "partial compliance" with its Busan agreement, but did not respond to detailed questions about other Asian trading partners. The Office of the US Trade Representative did not have immediate comment.

Trump's trade approach has damaged the country's reputation as a reliable trading partner, according to analysts and exporters, and spurred traditional trading partners to strike deals with rival exporters.

"Everybody else in the world is like, 'We are not going to follow Trump off the tariff cliff. We're not going to really retaliate against the United States, but we'll retaliate indirectly by lowering our barriers to everybody else'," Lincicome said.

Reporting by Karl Plume in Chicago. Editing by Emily Schmall and Rod Nickel

items.title: US DOJ antitrust division closes probe of NextEra Energy's acquisition of Dominion Energy
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department's antitrust division has decided to close its investigation of US power company NextEra Energy's (NEE.N) $66.8-billion acquisition of Dominion Energy (D.N), the department said in a statement on Thursday.

The merger plan unveiled by the US power companies in May will form one of the world's largest electric utilities during an expansion of energy-intensive data centers to support artificial intelligence.

Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Clarence Fernandez

items.title: Accused child sex predator Thomas Markle ruled competent to face trial
items.content_html:
TAMPA, Florida, Nov 19 (Reuters) - A US judge in Florida on Thursday declared Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, to be mentally competent to answer to a federal court charge accusing him of being a child sexual predator.

Accepting the findings of a court-appointed forensic psychiatrist, US Magistrate Judge Lindsay Griffin ruled the 82-year-old father-in-law of Prince Harry was mentally fit to understand the proceedings against him and to properly assist in his own defense, court records showed.

Neither prosecutors nor the defense disputed the findings of the psychiatrist's evaluation, contained in a 15-page report and based in large part on the doctor's in-person interview with Markle in prison last week.

Markle was charged November 5 in a criminal complaint with a single felony count of possessing child sexual abuse images.

According to an FBI affidavit filed with the complaint, the material in question, including two explicit photos of Markle posed with a naked underage girl and other images of him with children in various stages of undress, was found in two Los Angeles storage units.

Commenting on the case at the time of Markle's arrest on November 6 at an assisted-living center in Florida, FBI Director Kash Patel said Markle had "targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions."

Griffin's ruling capped a competency proceeding set in motion by the judge after Markle's first court hearing on the day of his arrest.

In ordering a psychiatric examination of the defendant, Griffin wrote that she found "reasonable cause" to believe Markle was suffering from some mental deficiency, based in part on his advanced age and "lack of recall" during his first court appearance the day of his arrest.

Dr. Aime Gerodimos, who conducted the evaluation, wrote in her report that Markle appeared to suffer from a "major neurocognitive disorder," possibly the result of mild vascular disease. She also found he was likely "exaggerating deficits" when asked to recall specifics of the allegations against him.

The psychiatrist concluded that Markle "does have sufficient present ability to understand the nature and consequences of the proceedings against him and to assist properly in his defense" — the legal standard for a criminal defendant to be deemed competent.

CASE ORIGINATED IN PHILIPPINES

Markle was first taken into custody at the assisted-living facility where he was residing in Lakeland, Florida, near Tampa. Griffin initially ordered him placed under home confinement on condition that Markle wear an electronic monitoring device.

But days later, the judge revoked the arrangement and ordered him back to jail without bond after Markle cut off his electronic ankle tag with a knife.

It remained unclear when Markle would be transferred to federal custody in California, where the case against him was lodged. The judge on Thursday set a preliminary hearing in the case for December 1 in Tampa.

According to the FBI affidavit, federal agents acting on a search warrant earlier this month seized a large cache of slides, film negatives and books from two storage lockers Markle had rented in Los Angeles since 2008.

One of the photos showed a naked girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines, where Markle previously resided and where authorities initiated an investigation of him last month, the affidavit said.

Philippine police said on Wednesday criminal complaints had been filed against Markle in the country's Cebu province, where he lived. The complaints accuse Markle of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, police said.

Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the claims were untrue and describing them as "sick lies."

Meghan Markle, an American actor, has been estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage to King Charles' younger son, Harry, in 2018, when the duchess has said she first became aware of the allegations against her father. She has said she was "deeply distressed" over the matter, which led her to cut off contact between her father and her two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5.

items.title: Trump ousts cyber director after tech outages spark criticism
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was fired from his job, a person close to the White House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking and national security systems.

President Donald Trump confirmed the firing at a news conference at the White House on Friday, saying he "didn't think that person was good enough."

The ouster comes as Trump and his administration face mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights. Next week will test the nation's technology systems, as millions of travelers take to the skies to visit loved ones for Thanksgiving and retailers prepare for a surge of Black Friday online shopping.

The dismissal of Cairncross is the administration's first major personnel move since the outages began.

Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.

"The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

Cairncross said in a statement on Thursday night it was the "honor of a lifetime to serve" in Trump's administration.

The recent technology disruptions are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. Advanced AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity protections.

The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can "share with the American people what's happening here."

Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. Congress established the position shortly before former President Joe Biden took office. Previous cyber directors had technology and national security experience.

His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.

Reporting by Courtney Rozen; Additional reporting by Bo Erickson and Kanishka Singh; Editing by Caitlin Webber, John Mair and Lincoln Feast.

items.title: Trump administration makes it easier for companies to classify workers as contractors
items.content_html:
Nov 19 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's administration unveiled a final rule on Thursday that will make it easier for companies in some industries to classify workers as independent contractors rather than their employees, who have more legal protections and can cost more.

The Department of Labor scrapped a rule adopted during the administration of former President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and replaced it with a legal test favored by business groups.

The new rule could lower costs for companies in a range of industries, including trucking, healthcare, retail sales and app-based transportation and delivery services such as Uber, that rely heavily on contractors. Such companies routinely face lawsuits accusing them of misclassifying workers to save money, which they deny.

The Labor Department said the 2024 rule was legally flawed and that the new test creates a clearer standard for businesses and workers to follow.

"It's more important than ever to ensure our labor regulations keep pace with the changing ways that Americans choose to work, and businesses choose to operate," Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said in a statement.

The rule will take effect in January, 60 days after it is formally published.

NEW RULE FOCUSES ON CONTROL

The Biden-era rule had established factors for determining whether a worker should be classified as an employee or contractor under federal wage law, and any one of them could tip the scales toward employee status.

The rule finalized on Thursday instead focuses on whether workers are under a company's control or have the opportunity for profit or loss based on their own initiative or investment.

Employees can cost businesses up to 30% more, according to several surveys, because they are entitled to the minimum wage, overtime pay, unemployment insurance, reimbursements for expenses and other protections not afforded to contractors.

Worker classification has been one of the most contentious employment-related issues over the last decade, and trade groups lobbied heavily to repeal the 2024 rule after an effort by Republicans in Congress to block it stalled.

The Biden-era rule had replaced a regulation adopted during Trump's first term that said workers who own their own businesses or can work for competing companies — such as a driver who works for Uber and Lyft — can be treated as contractors. The new rule is similar to that standard.

Supporters of the Biden-era rule have said misclassification of workers is rampant in some industries, and that repealing the rule would allow employers to strip workers of basic legal protections.

Reporting by Daniel Wiessner in Albany, New York, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Rod Nickel

items.title: Trump nominee to head Millennium Challenge aid agency vows to let data guide decisions
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Elliott Hulse, a former US Treasury official nominated to head the Millennium Challenge Corp (MCC), a US aid agency, on Thursday pledged to ensure that evidence-based data would guide decisions on future projects, if confirmed for the job.

Hulse, an adviser to the US executive director at the International Monetary Fund, served as acting assistant secretary of public affairs at the US Treasury before his nomination as chief executive of MCC. He worked at the World Bank from 2019 to 2025.

MCC had been targeted for closure during the early days of the Trump administration as part of a push to end foreign aid programs by Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency, but ultimately survived. Its budget, which had been around $900 million, was cut by nearly 11% in fiscal 2026, with further cuts proposed for 2027.

Hulse told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during a confirmation hearing that he would aim to build closer ties with Congress, the agency's board members and expand its external partnerships.

He also underscored the need to accelerate the timeline for approving new projects and not "leaving space for other countries or institutions to fill."

Senator Jacky Rosen, a Democrat, asked if Hulse would safeguard the agency's independence and base his decisions on data, noting that nearly a dozen MCC programs had been canceled under pressure from President Donald Trump's administration since January 2025.

"Certainly, if confirmed, I agree with you. The MCC scorecard should be driving all of its decisions, and I believe that data-driven approach is the right way forward," Hulse said.

The Trump administration has canceled MCC programs in several African countries, including Senegal, Kenya, Malawi and Togo, according to a report by the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service. It selected Ecuador, Guatemala and Bolivia for new programs, the report noted.

Pressed by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, top Democrat on the panel, on how MCC could ensure no "sweetheart deals" were made that could benefit someone in the US administration, Hulse reiterated his view that data should be the deciding factor.

"As I've emphasized to your colleague Senator Rosen, if confirmed, the scorecard is going to continue to drive every decision that I make," he said.

MCC awards assistance through a process based on countries' performance on a quantitative "scorecard" of indicators sourced from third-party organizations. To be considered, their per capita gross national income must fall under the World Bank's threshold for beginning negotiations to graduate from assistance, which was $8,105 in fiscal 2027.

Sub-Saharan Africa has been the top MCC recipient region to date, but no African countries were selected in 2025. The Trump administration also added "America First" and "America Returns" categories that CRS said were not authorized by US law.

Since its creation in 2004, MCC has signed 50 agreements for grants with 33 countries worth over $18 billion. Not all have been fully implemented, CRS noted.

Reporting by Andrea Shalal; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama
